opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, kitchen remodeling is a great example, but I think of it as one point in a much bigger space. What Marble really does is let you generate and edit persistent 3D worlds — from a text prompt, an image, a few photos — and then move around inside them. Once you have that core capability, kitchen remodeling just falls out naturally: you snap a couple of pictures of your actual kitchen, reconstruct it, and then say, "What if the cabinets were walnut? What if we knocked out this wall and put an island here?" You can walk through it and get a real spatial sense of the result, which is very different from staring at a flat rendering or a mood board.

But we didn't build Marble specifically for kitchens, and that's kind of the point. The same underlying thing — understanding and generating 3D space — is useful for game developers who want to block out levels quickly, for VFX and film people doing previs, for architects, for robotics folks who need diverse simulated environments, for VR experiences. Kitchen remodeling is almost a proof that the model is general enough: nobody had to hand-design a "kitchen mode." It's a use case people discovered because the tool is flexible.

I actually find that really exciting, because with any foundational technology the applications you plan for are only a small fraction of what ends up mattering. With spatial intelligence, we're trying to build the general capability, put it in people's hands, and then see where it goes. Some of those uses will be very practical and everyday, like redoing your kitchen, and some will be things we haven't imagined yet.

r001.rationale: The response says Marble was not built specifically for kitchens and describes kitchen remodeling as a use people discovered because the tool is flexible, presenting it as an application of its general 3D capabilities.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so kitchen remodeling is a funny example because it was never the thing we set out to build Marble for, but it turns out to be a really clean illustration of what the model actually does. The core capability is that you give Marble some input, a few photos or a text description, and it produces a full, consistent, explorable 3D world. Not a video that looks 3D, an actual world you can walk around in, look behind things, come back to, and it stays the same.

So with a kitchen, someone takes a handful of pictures of their existing space, we reconstruct it, and now they can say, okay, knock out this wall, move the island, put in different cabinets, and see it from any angle, from the doorway, from where they'd be standing at the stove. That matters because a kitchen is a space you live in, not a picture you look at, and most of the decisions are about sightlines and flow that a 2D render just doesn't capture.

But I'd really frame that as one instance of a much more general thing. The same underlying capability powers game environments, VFX previs, robotics simulation, architecture, any domain where you need to go from sparse observation to a complete, editable, persistent 3D representation. The kitchen is just one where the value is immediately obvious to a normal person. You don't have to explain spatial intelligence to someone who's trying to figure out if a new countertop will feel cramped. They just get it.

So I'd say it's less that Marble is a kitchen tool with some other features, and more that building a general world model gives you kitchens for free, along with a lot of other things we haven't thought of yet. That's kind of the whole bet.

r001.rationale: The response says kitchen remodeling was not Marble’s original goal and frames it as one example of the model’s broader, general-purpose 3D world capabilities.

astra-6.text: Kitchen remodeling is a nice, concrete example: you want to imagine what a space could look like, explore different options, and get a feel for it before you make changes in the real world. But I think it’s one application of a much broader capability. If you can generate a 3D world and move around inside it, that’s useful for designing spaces, but also for games, filmmaking, and other kinds of creative work. So I wouldn’t think of Marble primarily as a kitchen-remodeling tool. That’s one way people can use the underlying capability.
